newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks close higher, helped by blue chips. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks close higher, helped by blue chips. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]

text.p: Tokyo stocks bounced back on Tuesday and closed higher for the first time in four days. The recent falls sparked bargain-hunting in global blue-chip issues which started to become more attractive, such as Fujitsu Ltd and Sony Corp, brokers said.
The key Nikkei 225 average finished up 461.67 points, or 2.66 percent, at 17,796.57, the day's highest level. It had fallen to 17,195.25 at one stage.
Its March futures closed 410 points higher at 17,790.
"The recent bearish sectors seem to have been sold off enough for now," said Masaaki Higashida, deputy general manager at Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
The market has been suffering from an uncertain picture of the country's near-term economic growth and lingering woes in the financial industry.
"The Nikkei 225 is likely to test the upside until it meets with sell orders, aiming to take profits ahead of corporate book closings (at the end of March)," he said.
The leading issue in Tuesday's rebound was Fujitsu, which climbed to its highest level in one year in heavy trade.
The share price of the computer maker gained 30 yen to end at 1,220 yen, its highest level since January 5 last year.
Its turnover of 13.52 million shares made it the most active on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
"High-tech shares are attractive in the current (vulnerable) market. Fujitsu is a core issue in that area," said a broker at a major Japanese securities house.
Brokers also said that the rise was triggered by Nomura Research Institute Ltd's upgrading of the firm.
Sony, briefly jumping above 8,000 yen for the first time in more than six years, also reinforced the Nikkei 225's recovery.

Brokers said the possibility of the global consumer electronics maker entering the satellite business attracted investors. Sony's share price ended up 160 yen at 7,990 yen, after briefly hitting 8,010 yen.
Turnover on the Tokyo bourse's first section was still moderate at 397 million shares on Tuesday, up slightly from Monday's 348 million shares.
Gainers outnumbered losers 797 to 315 issues, while 128 issues were unchanged.
Meanwhile, the broader-based TOPIX index closed modestly higher, gaining 19.28 points or 1.45 percent.
Brokers said that the limited gains in the bank-studded TOPIX index reflected the weakness in the financial sector.

"Banking and brokerage will be the main sectors to suffer sales ahead of the end-March book closings, and the market won't be able to post a strong rally until these sectors start to recover," Nomura's Higashida said.
The recent trend of weakening companies' mutual shares holdings is likely to prompt further sales in bank and brokerage shares later this month or in February, brokers said.
"Today's rebound doesn't mean that downside risks in the market have disappeared," one analyst said.
There are lingering worries in the market over banks, saddled with huge problem loans, as they are also expected to face fierce competition under planned financial reforms.
On Tuesday, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka ruled out the possibility of Japan using more public funds to help resolve the bad loan problems at financial institutions.
Mitsuzuka said: "We have stated that we will not use public funds for the bad loan problems at nonbank financial institutions. It is the same for other institutions."
His comment followed Monday's remark from a key member of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party.
The LDP official was reported to have said he was in favour of using more public money to help resolve their debt problems.
In other indices, the second section index was down 7.08 points to end at 1,719.12, with 6.08 million shares traded.
The over-the-counter (OTC) index was also down, losing 8.03 points to 1,205.68.

Among sectors, gainers (corrects from "decliners") were led by mining, warehousing, transportation equipment, miscellaneous manufacturing and real estate. The only major declining sector was communications.
(Corrects to make clear communications sector was declining not gaining).
-- Hiroko Nakata, Tokyo Equities Desk +81-3-3432-8027 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
